Fundamental — what it's worth: A weighted what-if off the published fair value — not a re-run DCF, and it never touches the Monte Carlo section below. The sizes come from the study’s own sensitivity grids, each of which re-runs the whole unit build, scaled down for the fact that only the cash-flow lenses move. Note which lever dominates: the cost of capital, not the operations. Three points of easing is worth more than a fifteen-percent swing in conversion margin, because 77% of the enterprise value sits in the terminal year and the Egyptian discount rate is what compresses it. That is the study’s central claim in one control.
Technical & price structure: In plain terms: at today’s 21.5% cost of capital the discounted cash flows are worth about EGP 3.8bn while the net debt against them is about EGP 9.8bn — so on the base case the equity is worth nothing, and is floored at zero only because a shareholder cannot owe more than the stake. What EGP 2.19 buys is an option on three things going right together: the receivables collecting, conversion margins recovering from the 1Q26 trough, and the CBE resuming its easing cycle. That’s the bet.
Monte Carlo — where could the price go?: Our fundamental range tops out at EGP 0.95 even in the bull case — so unlike most names we cover, the whole simulated price cone sits ABOVE the fair-value range, not around it. Read that gap for what it is: the simulation prices where the tape can travel over three months, the study prices what the business is worth. A sustained move above EGP 0.95 on the fundamentals — collection landing, margins recovering, rates falling — is the point where we’d rebuild the study.

One Monte Carlo model, 50,000 paths, driven by the outside forces relevant to a hard-currency industrial exporter listed in a soft-currency market: the LME copper price, the EGP/USD path, the CBE policy corridor and the pace of easing, Egyptian inflation, Gulf and North African grid and infrastructure spending, the order book and its conversion rate, interconnector and data-centre demand for cable and transformers, energy and freight costs, convertibility and repatriation risk on the foreign earnings, and the free float — 11.6% of the shares, with 68% held by the family and 20% by Electra, which is what makes the tape thin. How is the ARCC valuation calculated? — The study uses an instrument-appropriate lens — a three-statement FCFF DCF built bottom-up on three disclosed product lines with a PER-TONNE COST STACK \u2014 feedstock, energy, chemicals and fixed conversion charged separately, so the gross margin (blended and per line) is an output rather than an input, cross-checked against normalized earnings power, relative EV/EBITDA and a justified price-to-book — combined with a 50,000-path Monte Carlo simulation that expresses the result as a probability distribution.
